nodes.name: WO3 nanoarray hydrothermal synthesis
nodes.procedure: With magnetic stirring, tungstic acid powder (0.625 g) was dissolved in 20 ml 12 wt.% hydrogen peroxide solution by heating at 95°C for 3 h. Then, the solution was transferred into a Teflon reaction kettle with 0.2 g anhydrous sodium sulfate, 115 μl hydrochloric acid, and a piece of 2 cm × 2 cm CFP added in. WO3 nanoarrays were obtained after being heated for 12 h at 180°C.

nodes.source_text: Synthesis of WO3 nanoarrays. WO3 nanoarrays on CFP were synthesized by the hydrothermal method. With magnetic stirring, tungstic acid powder (0.625 g) was dissolved in 20 ml 12 wt.% hydrogen peroxide solution by heating at 95°C for 3 h. Then, the solution was transferred into a Teflon reaction kettle with 0.2 g anhydrous sodium sulfate, 115 μl hydrochloric acid, and a piece of 2 cm × 2 cm CFP added in. WO3 nanoarrays were obtained after being heated for 12 h at 180°C

nodes.name: N-WC nanoarray chemical vapor deposition
nodes.procedure: WO3 nanoarrays on a combustion boat that containing melamine was heated at 850°C for 3 h, with Ar gas flowing in a tube furnace.

nodes.name: WO3 powder hydrothermal synthesis
nodes.procedure: WO3 powder without nanoarray structure was synthesized by the same hydrothermal method as WO3 nanoarrays but without CFP: tungstic acid powder (0.625 g) was dissolved in 20 ml 12 wt.% hydrogen peroxide solution by heating at 95°C for 3 h. Then, the solution was transferred into a Teflon reaction kettle with 0.2 g anhydrous sodium sulfate, 115 μl hydrochloric acid. WO3 powder was obtained after being heated for 12 h at 180°C.

nodes.source_text: N-WC nanoarray shows the most impressive HER activity with small overpotentials of -89 mV at current density of -10 mA cm⁻² and -190 mV overpotential at -200 mA cm⁻² (Fig. 4a)... Tafel slope of N-WC nanoarray for HER is 75 mV dec⁻¹ (Fig. 4b)... charge transfer resistance of 0.5 ohms at -0.5 V vs RHE (Fig. 4c)
The WC nanoarray exhibits -200 mA cm⁻² at -320 mV (Fig. 4a)
After doping with nitrogen, the N-WC electrode shows much improved catalytic behavior, with -113 mV overpotential to drive catalytic current of -10 mA cm⁻² and -310 mV overpotential for -200 mA cm⁻²
The WC electrode exhibits catalytic performance with overpotential of -193 mV at -10 mA cm⁻² and -513 mV at -200 mA cm⁻²

OER starts at about 1.35 V on N-WC nanoarray electrode... At about 1.7 V vs. RHE, the current density reaches up to 60 mA cm⁻² (Fig. 6a)... O₂ concentration rises up to 1.5, 1.6, and 1.7 ppm (Fig. 6b)... potential increases from 1.35 to 1.54 V vs. RHE after 1 h (Fig. 6c)

nodes.characterization_summary: WO3 nanoarray shows thin belt nanoarray structure ~5 μm long, ~400 nm wide, ~10 nm thick. N-WC nanoarray maintains this morphology but becomes 2-3 nm thinner.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 2b shows the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of WO₃ grown on CFP, which exhibits a nanoarray structure composed of thin belts, with about 5 μm long, ∼400 nm wide, and ∼10 nm thick. The morphology of WO₃ was well maintained after being converted to N-WC nanoarray (Fig. 2c) except for becoming 2-3 nm thinner.

nodes.characterization_summary: N-WC nanoarray shows hexagonal WC phase (PDF#51-0939) with peak at 42.5° from tetragonal carbon (PDF#54-0501); WO3 nanoarray matches hexagonal WO3 (PDF#75-2187).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 3a displays the X-ray diffraction (XRD) data of CFP, WO₃ nanoarray, and N-WC nanoarray... After reduction and carbonization of WO₃, hexagonal WC phase (PDF#51-0939) was successfully prepared as shown in the XRD pattern of N-WC nanoarray.

nodes.characterization_summary: N-WC nanoarray belts consist of parallel narrow belts with surface nanoparticles ~3 nm diameter.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of Fig. 3b show that each N-WC belt consists of parallel narrow belts arrayed side by side.

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM shows 0.25 nm d-spacing corresponding to (100) planes of hexagonal WC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image shows the lattice fringes of the nanoparticles. The 0.25 nm d-spacing corresponds to the (100) planes of hexagonal WC.

nodes.characterization_summary: N-WC nanoarray surface N content 8.0 at.%; N 1s peaks: 398.7 eV (N-W bonding), 399.7 eV and 401.3 eV (N-C bonds); W 4f: W-N bonds at 35.5/38 eV, W-C bonds at 32.5/34.6 eV, surface W oxidation at 41.3 eV.
nodes.evidence_snippet: From the XPS data in Fig. 3c, the N element can be identified and the content at the surface of the sample is about 8.0 at.%. Figure 3d displays N 1s high-resolution XPS profile. The fitting peaks at 399.7 and 401.3 eV can be assigned to features of N–C bonds, and the peak at 398.7 eV has been reported to represent N-W bonding. The presence of the N–W bond is also supported by the W 4f XPS in Fig. 3e.

nodes.characterization_summary: TEM-EDS shows uniform N distribution along N-WC nanobelts with N content 6.6 at.%; tungsten and carbon are main components.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 3f and Supplementary Table 1 show the TEM-EDS result... As shown in elemental mapping, N is uniformly distributed along the N-WC nanobelts... According to the TEM-EDS result, the N content is about 6.6 at.%

nodes.characterization_summary: SAED shows WC (001) and WC (100) diffraction rings confirming hexagonal WC phase.
nodes.evidence_snippet: WC (001) and WC (100) diffraction rings could be clearly seen in the SAED image (Supplementary Fig. 4).

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM-EDS mapping shows tungsten and carbon as main components of N-WC nanoarray with very small amount of nitrogen.
nodes.evidence_snippet: From SEM-energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) mapping displayed in Supplementary Fig. 5, tungsten and carbon are the main components of N-WC nanoarray with only a very small amount of nitrogen.

nodes.characterization_summary: WC nanoarray, N-WC nanoarray, N-WC powder, and WC powder all show pure hexagonal WC phase (PDF#51-0939).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Supplementary Fig. 6 shows XRD patterns of CFP, N-WC nanoarray, N-WC, and WC nanoarray. All of them behave as pure phases of WC (PDF#51-0939).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS confirms absence of nitrogen in WC nanoarray.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The EDS of WC nanoarray in Supplementary Fig. 7 shows the absence of nitrogen.

nodes.characterization_summary: Post-OER N-WC nanoarray shows small amount of tungsten oxides formed.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To acquire the reason for the instability of N-WC nanoarray, we recorded the XRD patterns of N-WC nanoarray before and after OER test, showing that a small amount of tungsten oxides formed on N-WC nanoarray during OER test (Fig. 6d).
